## The senior bar

What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

- Chooses among prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning and training by what the failure actually is (missing knowledge, wrong behaviour, cost), and states the evaluation that would show the choice was right.
- Writes the objectives from memory (next-token loss, LoRA update, preference losses, distillation, contrastive loss) and explains each term's purpose and failure mode.
- Treats data as the main lever, with a concrete view on formatting, masking, deduplication, contamination and the mix that prevents forgetting.
- Knows what optimising a learned reward or judge does to a model and builds the checks that catch over-optimisation.
- Reasons about compute with arithmetic, from tokens and parameters to GPU-days, and about what small-scale results do and do not predict at larger scale.
- Separates what is established from what is contested or changing quickly, and says which is which.

<details class="qa" id="llm-001">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> How is a decoder-only language model trained, and how does that differ from how it is used at inference? Define perplexity while you are at it.</summary>

**Training.** The model defines a distribution over the next token given the previous
ones, and is trained by maximum likelihood on text:

$$\mathcal L(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}).$$

A causal attention mask lets one forward pass compute the prediction at every position
at once, each conditioned on the true previous tokens (**teacher forcing**). A sequence
of $T$ tokens therefore yields $T$ training signals for the cost of one pass, which is
why pretraining is efficient.

**Inference.** Generation is sequential: sample or pick a token from
$p_\theta(\cdot \mid x_{<t})$, append it, and repeat. The model now conditions on its own
outputs, a distribution it never saw in training, so early errors can compound. Each
new token needs a forward pass (made cheap by caching keys and values), so cost grows
with output length.

**Perplexity** is the exponential of the average loss, $\mathrm{PPL} = e^{\mathcal L}$:
the effective number of equally likely choices per token. Loss divided by $\ln 2$ is
bits per token, which makes the link to compression explicit.

Things to say about it:

- It is comparable only between models with the same tokenizer and the same evaluation
  text. A tokenizer with shorter tokens gets lower per-token loss for the same quality.
- It measures fit to the text distribution, not usefulness. A model can improve
  perplexity while getting worse at following instructions, and post-training often
  raises perplexity on raw text.
- It is still the cleanest signal during pretraining, and held-out loss against training
  loss shows memorisation.

Nothing in the objective mentions truth, helpfulness or instructions. Those behaviours
come from the data and from post-training.

**Follow-ups**

- Why can you not compare the perplexity of two models with different tokenizers?
- What is exposure bias, and why does it matter less for large models than the argument suggests?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-002">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Compare encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder transformers. Decoder-only models dominate; when would you still choose one of the others?</summary>

| Family | Attention | Trained with | Natural use |
|-|-|-|-|
| Encoder-only (BERT family) | Bidirectional: every token sees the whole input | Masked-token prediction, or contrastive objectives for embeddings | Understanding tasks: classification, tagging, retrieval embeddings, reranking |
| Decoder-only (GPT family) | Causal: each token sees only the past | Next-token prediction | Generation, and with prompting almost any task |
| Encoder-decoder (T5 family) | Bidirectional encoder; causal decoder with cross-attention to the encoder | Sequence-to-sequence objectives, such as span corruption | Transduction: translation, summarisation, speech recognition |

**Why decoder-only won for general models.** One objective that uses every token of any
text, one stack that is simple to scale, a single interface (text in, text out) that
unifies tasks, and prefix caching at inference. In-context learning made task-specific
heads unnecessary.

**When to choose an encoder.**

- High-volume classification, retrieval or reranking with tight latency and cost. An
  encoder with a few hundred million parameters, fine-tuned, processes an input in one
  pass with no generation loop, and is orders of magnitude cheaper per item than
  prompting a large generative model.
- Embeddings. Bidirectional context gives better representations per parameter,
  although decoder-based embedding models with modified attention or pooling are now
  competitive at larger sizes.
- Token-level tasks (entity tagging, span extraction) where an output per input token is
  wanted.

**When to choose an encoder-decoder.** The input is long and fixed and the output is
short, or the input is a different modality: the encoder runs once, and the decoder
attends to it. Speech recognition and many translation systems use this shape.

The practical pattern in products is a cascade: a small encoder model handles the bulk
of traffic and routes hard cases to a large generative model, often trained on labels
that the large model produced.

**Follow-ups**

- Why is a bidirectional encoder a poor generator?
- You need to classify 100 million documents a day. Sketch the model choice and the cost argument.

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-003">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Why do language models hallucinate? Answer from the training side: what in the objective, the data and the evaluation produces confident false statements?</summary>

Several causes stack.

- **The pretraining objective rewards plausibility.** The model learns which
  continuations are likely in text. For a fact it has seen often, the likely
  continuation is the true one. For a rare fact (an obscure person's birthday, a
  citation), many continuations are about equally plausible in form, and the model
  produces one of them. Fluent, well-formed and wrong is exactly what a good density
  model outputs when it lacks the specific knowledge.
- **The data rarely demonstrates abstention.** Written text mostly contains assertions;
  authors who do not know something tend not to write about it. So "I don't know" is an
  unlikely continuation by default.
- **Knowledge is not separated from guessing internally in a way the output must
  respect.** The same generation mechanism serves both. Models do carry signals about
  their own uncertainty, but nothing forces the text to reflect them.
- **Post-training incentives.** If raters or reward models prefer complete, confident
  answers, and evaluations score a correct guess above an abstention and a wrong guess
  no worse than one, then training and model selection both push toward guessing.
- **Conditioning errors.** A question with a false premise, a long context with
  conflicting passages, or the model's own earlier mistake pulls the continuation
  along.
- **Decoding.** Sampling adds variance, but greedy decoding does not remove the problem.

What follows for mitigation:

- Provide the knowledge at inference (retrieval, tools) and train the model to rely on
  and cite it.
- Train and evaluate abstention explicitly: reward "I don't know" on unanswerable items
  and penalise confident errors more than abstentions.
- Verify outputs against sources, or with a second pass, where the cost of an error is
  high.

A measured view to state: hallucination rates fall with model scale and with grounding,
but the incentive problem means it does not vanish by scale alone.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you build an evaluation that does not reward guessing?
- Why does retrieval reduce hallucination but not eliminate it?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-004">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> A model does not perform well enough on your task. How do you decide between better prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning and training your own model?</summary>

Diagnose the failure first; each tool fixes a different one.

| Failure | Tool |
|-|-|
| The model can do it but was not told clearly what is wanted | Prompting: instructions, examples, output format, decomposition |
| The model lacks facts that are private, recent or too many to memorise | Retrieval or tools: put the facts in the context at request time |
| The model knows enough but behaves wrongly or inconsistently: style, format, a narrow skill, a domain's conventions | Fine-tuning |
| The task is fine but cost or latency is too high | Fine-tune or distil a smaller model on the large model's outputs |
| The domain is far from anything in the model's training data (a new modality, a specialised notation) | Continued pretraining, or training a model |

**Order of attempts.** Cheapest and most reversible first:

1. Build an evaluation set and measure the baseline. Without it nothing else can be
   judged.
2. Prompting, including few-shot examples. Hours of work, no infrastructure.
3. Retrieval, if error analysis shows missing knowledge.
4. Fine-tuning, if errors remain that examples could teach and you have, or can create,
   hundreds to thousands of good examples.
5. Training from scratch almost never; it needs a reason that survives the question
   "why not adapt an existing model?".

**What fine-tuning costs beyond compute.** A training set to build and maintain, an
evaluation and regression process, a model to host or a provider's tuning service to
depend on, and repeated work whenever the base model is upgraded. It also does not
reliably add facts: a tuned model still hallucinates details it saw a few times, so
knowledge belongs in retrieval.

**Combinations are normal.** Retrieval for knowledge plus a fine-tune for format and
tone; a prompt-engineered large model generating data to tune a small one.

The senior signal is error analysis: reading 50 failures and sorting them by cause
before choosing.

**Follow-ups**

- You have 200 labelled examples. Is that enough to fine-tune, and how would you find out?
- Why is fine-tuning a poor way to add new facts?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-005">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Open-weights model that you host, or a proprietary model behind an API? How do you decide for a product?</summary>

Decide per workload, on quality, control, cost and risk.

**Quality on your task.** Measure candidates on your own evaluation set. The strongest
proprietary models usually lead on hard reasoning and long agentic tasks; for narrower
tasks (extraction, classification, routine generation) a smaller open model, especially
fine-tuned, is often equal.

**Control.**

- *Customisation.* Open weights allow any fine-tuning, quantization, constrained
  decoding or change to the serving stack. APIs offer what the provider exposes.
- *Stability.* A hosted model can be updated or retired on the provider's schedule;
  weights you hold do not change. Pinning versions mitigates but does not remove this.
- *Data.* Self-hosting keeps data inside your environment, which some customers and
  regulations require. Providers offer contractual and regional controls that satisfy
  many but not all cases.

**Cost.**

- API: pay per token, no fixed cost, scales to zero. Best for low or spiky volume.
- Self-hosted: you pay for GPUs whether used or not, plus engineers to run them. It wins
  at high, steady utilisation, or when a small model replaces a large one. Compare cost
  per task at your real utilisation, including on-call and upgrades.

**Latency.** Self-hosting allows co-location, dedicated capacity and a small specialised
model; APIs add network time and shared-capacity variance but need no tuning.

**Risk.** Provider dependency and outages against operational burden; licence terms of
open models, which vary and may restrict commercial use; security review either way.

**Common outcome.** Both. A proprietary frontier model for the hardest steps and for
generating training data, open or small models for high-volume narrow steps, behind one
internal interface so that each call site can be re-routed when prices or models
change. Re-evaluate on a schedule, because the trade moves every few months.

**Follow-ups**

- At what request volume does hosting a small open model become cheaper than an API for your use case?
- What would you put in the abstraction layer between your product and the model?

</details>

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.finetuning.3"> Format chat data with the model's template and mask the loss to the response tokens

<details class="qa" id="llm-009">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Explain LoRA. What is the update, how many parameters does it train, and why are the initialisation and the scaling chosen the way they are?</summary>

LoRA freezes the pretrained weight matrix $W \in \mathbb R^{d \times k}$ and learns a
low-rank correction:

$$W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}\, B A, \qquad B \in \mathbb R^{d \times r},\ A \in \mathbb R^{r \times k},\ r \ll \min(d, k).$$

Only $A$ and $B$ are trained.

**Parameter count.** $r(d + k)$ per adapted matrix instead of $dk$. For $d = k = 4096$
and $r = 8$: 65 536 against 16.8 million, about 0.4%. Because the base weights receive no
gradient, there is no optimizer state for them, which is where the memory saving in
training comes from.

**Initialisation.** $A$ is random and $B$ is zero, so $BA = 0$ at the start and training
begins exactly from the pretrained model.

**Scaling.** The factor $\alpha / r$ keeps the size of the update roughly comparable when
the rank is changed, so that the learning rate need not be retuned for every $r$. A
variant scales by $\alpha / \sqrt r$, which behaves better at high rank.

**Why low rank is enough.** The hypothesis, supported empirically, is that the weight
change needed to adapt a pretrained model to a task has low intrinsic rank.

**Properties in use.**

- *No inference overhead.* $BA$ can be merged into $W$ after training.
- *Cheap to store and swap.* An adapter is megabytes; many can share one base model in
  serving.
- *Choices.* Which matrices to adapt (attention projections at minimum; all linear
  layers usually works better), the rank (4 to 64 is typical; higher for tasks far from
  the base model), $\alpha$, and dropout on the adapter input.
- *QLoRA.* The frozen base is loaded in 4-bit precision and the adapters are trained in
  higher precision on top, which lets large models be tuned on a single GPU.

**Limits.** For tasks needing large changes to the model (a new language, a big shift
in behaviour, large data) full fine-tuning can still be better, and LoRA is more
sensitive to the learning rate than its simplicity suggests.

**Follow-ups**

- Why initialise B to zero and not both matrices randomly?
- How would you serve 500 different LoRA adapters efficiently?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-010">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Implement a LoRA wrapper for a linear layer in PyTorch, including merging the adapter into the base weight.</summary>

```python
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base: nn.Linear, r: int = 8, alpha: float = 16.0,
                 dropout: float = 0.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base
        for p in self.base.parameters():
            p.requires_grad_(False)                  # freeze W and bias
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(r, base.in_features))
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, r))
        nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.A, a=math.sqrt(5))
        self.scale = alpha / r
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.merged = False

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.base(x)
        if not self.merged:
            out = out + self.scale * (self.drop(x) @ self.A.T @ self.B.T)
        return out

    @torch.no_grad()
    def merge(self):
        if not self.merged:
            self.base.weight += self.scale * (self.B @ self.A)
            self.merged = True
```

What an interviewer checks:

- **Shapes.** `x @ A.T` maps `[..., in]` to `[..., r]`, then `@ B.T` to `[..., out]`. The
  product `B @ A` has the shape of `base.weight`, `[out, in]`.
- **Zero start.** `B` is zero, so the wrapped layer initially computes exactly what the
  base layer does.
- **Freezing.** Only `A` and `B` require gradients; pass only those to the optimizer, and
  verify the count of trainable parameters.
- **Compute the low-rank path as two small products**, never by forming the full
  `B @ A` in the forward pass.
- **Dropout applies to the adapter path only**, and must be inactive when merged.
- **Merging** removes the extra latency. After merging into a quantised or
  half-precision base, check outputs, since the small update can be lost to rounding.

To apply it to a model, walk the modules and replace the chosen `nn.Linear` layers (for
example the attention projections) with the wrapper. Save only the adapter's state, and
record the base model's exact identifier with it, because an adapter is meaningless on
a different base.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you unmerge the adapter?
- What changes for a convolution or an embedding layer?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-011">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Compare full fine-tuning, LoRA-style adapters and prompt or prefix tuning. How do you choose?</summary>

| Method | Trains | Training cost | Serving | Quality |
|-|-|-|-|-|
| Full fine-tuning | All weights | Highest: gradients and optimizer state for everything; needs the most memory | One full model copy per task | Highest ceiling, especially with much data or a large shift from the base |
| Adapters (LoRA and variants) | Small low-rank matrices, typically well under 1% of parameters | Low memory for optimizer state; the forward and backward pass through the frozen model is still paid | Merge for zero overhead, or keep separate and share one base among many adapters | Close to full fine-tuning on most tasks |
| Prompt or prefix tuning | A few learned vectors prepended to the input or to each layer | Lowest parameter count | No weight changes; consumes context positions | Usually below adapters; sensitive to initialisation and harder to optimise |

**Choose full fine-tuning when** you have a lot of data, the target differs greatly from
the base (a new language, a new modality, a large behavioural change), you serve a
single model anyway, and you can afford the compute. It is also the norm for small
models, where the cost is trivial.

**Choose adapters when** compute or memory is limited, you need many task- or
customer-specific variants on one base, you want to limit drift from the base model,
or you iterate often. This is the default for adapting large open models.

**Prompt tuning** is rarely the best choice now, except where the model's weights cannot
be touched but embeddings can.

Points that cut across the table:

- *Forgetting.* Full fine-tuning on narrow data damages general abilities more readily;
  adapters constrain the change, though they do not eliminate forgetting.
- *Hyperparameters.* Adapters want a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning (often
  around $10^{-4}$ against $10^{-5}$), and rank and target modules matter.
- *Operations.* Every method ties you to a specific base checkpoint. When the base is
  upgraded, all tuned variants must be retrained and re-evaluated, so keep the data and
  the pipeline, not only the weights.
- *Hosted fine-tuning* services make the choice for you; evaluate the result as you
  would any model.

Whatever the method, the data and the evaluation decide the outcome more than the
choice of method does.

**Follow-ups**

- Why does LoRA reduce optimizer memory but not the cost of the forward pass?
- Your base model is replaced by a newer version. What do you have to redo?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-012">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> You fine-tune a chat model on conversation data. Training loss falls nicely, but at inference the model rambles, never stops, or answers worse than before tuning. What are the likely data-formatting causes?</summary>

Most failures of supervised fine-tuning are formatting errors between how the data was
rendered for training and what the model sees at inference.

**1. Chat template mismatch.** Each chat model was trained with a specific template: role
markers, turn separators and special tokens. Training with one rendering and serving
with another puts the model off-distribution. Use the tokenizer's own chat template for
both, and print a fully rendered example, with special tokens visible, from each path.

**2. Missing end-of-turn token in the targets.** If the response's end token is not
included in the labels, the model never learns to stop and runs on until the length
limit. Check that the last supervised token of each response is the end-of-turn or
end-of-sequence token, and that generation is configured to stop on it.

**3. Loss on the wrong tokens.** The loss should cover only the assistant's tokens.
Training on the system prompt and user turns teaches the model to imitate users and
wastes capacity. Set the labels of all other positions to the ignore index, and verify
the mask on a sample by decoding only the supervised tokens.

**4. Special tokens as plain text.** Role markers typed as strings may be split into
ordinary sub-tokens instead of the single special token id. Compare token ids, not
strings.

**5. Duplicate or missing beginning-of-sequence token**, when both the template and the
tokenizer add one.

**6. Truncation.** Long examples cut at the maximum length lose the response or its
ending. Count how many examples are truncated and where.

**7. Padding.** Pad tokens must be masked in attention and in the loss. For batched
generation with a decoder-only model, pad on the left, or the model continues from pad
tokens.

**8. Data content.** Responses in the data that are themselves long or unfinished, or a
system prompt in training that is absent at inference.

The habit that prevents all of these: before any long run, overfit a handful of
examples and generate from them through the real inference path.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you verify that the loss mask covers exactly the assistant tokens?
- Why must padding be on the left for batched generation?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-013">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> After fine-tuning, your model is better on the target task's test set but users report it has become worse at other things. How do you diagnose and fix it?</summary>

Two different problems hide behind this report, and the evaluation must separate them.

**1. Forgetting.** Training on narrow data moved the weights away from what supported
general abilities: other languages, reasoning, instruction-following outside the tuned
format, refusals and safety behaviour.

**2. Overfitting to the format of the data.** The model learned surface features of the
training set: a fixed response length, a tone, always producing a certain structure,
always answering instead of asking for clarification. It then applies them everywhere.

**Diagnose.**

- Run a *retention suite* on the base and tuned model: general benchmarks, a sample of
  real traffic outside the target task, safety checks. Compare by category.
- Compare outputs side by side on prompts unrelated to the task. Format overfitting is
  visible at a glance.
- Check the target test set for leakage or near-duplicates of training data; an inflated
  task metric may be part of the story.
- Plot retention metrics against training steps from saved checkpoints. Forgetting
  usually grows with steps, and an earlier checkpoint may give most of the task gain at
  little cost.

**Fix, least invasive first.**

- Train less: fewer epochs, lower learning rate, early stopping on a combined criterion.
- Mix in general data: a share of diverse instruction data, or outputs of the base model
  on general prompts, so that the model keeps rehearsing its old behaviour.
- Constrain the update: adapters with modest rank instead of full fine-tuning, or weight
  averaging between the base and tuned weights.
- Diversify the task data: vary formats, lengths and phrasings, and include examples
  where the right behaviour is to decline or ask.
- Route instead of merge: keep the tuned model for the task and the base model for
  everything else.

**Process change.** Make the retention suite a release gate alongside the task metric,
so that the trade is seen before users see it.

**Follow-ups**

- What goes into a retention suite for a customer-support fine-tune?
- How does mixing in the base model's own outputs help?

</details>


### Multimodal / vision-language models <span class="demand">18% of postings</span> {#multimodal}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.multimodal.0"> Write the symmetric contrastive loss of CLIP and say what the model does and does not learn
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.multimodal.1"> Describe a vision-language model as encoder, projector and language model, with its training stages
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.multimodal.2"> Compare continuous embeddings with discrete tokens for non-text modalities
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.multimodal.3"> Diagnose a vision-language model that answers from language priors instead of the image

<details class="qa" id="llm-027">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Explain how CLIP is trained. Write the loss, and say what such a model is good at and where it fails.</summary>

CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so that matching image-caption pairs
are close in a shared embedding space and non-matching pairs are far apart.

**Loss.** For a batch of $N$ pairs, compute L2-normalised embeddings $u_i$ (image) and
$v_i$ (text) and the matrix of scaled cosine similarities
$s_{ij} = u_i^\top v_j / \tau$, with a learned temperature $\tau$. Each image should pick
out its own caption among the $N$ in the batch, and each caption its own image:

$$\mathcal L = \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ -\log \frac{e^{s_{ii}}}{\sum_j e^{s_{ij}}} \;-\; \log \frac{e^{s_{ii}}}{\sum_j e^{s_{ji}}} \right].$$

```python
logits = logit_scale * image_emb @ text_emb.T          # [N, N], embeddings normalised
labels = torch.arange(len(logits), device=logits.device)
loss = (F.cross_entropy(logits, labels) + F.cross_entropy(logits.T, labels)) / 2
```

The other items in the batch are the negatives, so the batch size sets how hard the
task is, which is why these models are trained with very large batches. A sigmoid
variant scores each pair independently and removes the dependence on a batch-wide
softmax.

**What it is good at.**

- Zero-shot classification: embed the class names as text ("a photo of a dog") and pick
  the nearest to the image embedding.
- Retrieval in both directions, and as a general visual backbone whose features align
  with language, which is why it became the standard vision encoder for
  vision-language models.
- Robustness to distribution shift compared with models trained on fixed label sets.

**Where it fails.**

- *Composition.* It behaves much like a bag of concepts: "a red cube on a blue sphere"
  and the reverse get similar embeddings. Counting, spatial relations and attribute
  binding are weak.
- *Fine detail and text in images*, limited by input resolution and by a single global
  embedding.
- *False negatives.* Two captions in a batch may both fit an image, but one is treated
  as wrong.
- *Data bias.* It inherits the biases and noise of web image-text pairs.
- *Prompt sensitivity* in zero-shot use; templates and ensembling of prompts matter.

**Follow-ups**

- Why does the batch size matter so much for contrastive training?
- What does the learned temperature do, and what happens if it is fixed too high?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-028">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> How does a vision-language model feed an image to a language model? Describe the architecture, the cost in tokens, and the usual training stages.</summary>

**Architecture.** The common design has three parts.

1. A **vision encoder**, usually a vision transformer pretrained contrastively, splits
   the image into patches and outputs one embedding per patch.
2. A **projector** maps those embeddings into the language model's input embedding
   space. It is a small MLP in the simplest designs, or a resampler with cross-attention
   that compresses many patch embeddings into a fixed, smaller number.
3. The **language model** receives the projected image embeddings as if they were token
   embeddings, interleaved with the text tokens, and generates text as usual.

The language model never sees pixels. It sees a sequence of vectors that occupy
positions in its context.

**Token cost.** The number of image tokens is the number of patches. With 14-pixel
patches at 336 by 336 resolution that is $24 \times 24 = 576$ tokens per image. Higher
resolution is usually handled by tiling the image into several crops plus a
low-resolution overview, which multiplies the count, so a detailed document page can
cost thousands of tokens. Resolution is therefore a direct trade between visual detail
and context, latency and price. Resamplers and token pooling exist to cut that cost.

**Training stages** in the widely used recipe:

1. *Alignment.* Freeze the vision encoder and the language model and train only the
   projector on image-caption pairs, so that image embeddings land where the language
   model can read them.
2. *Instruction tuning.* Train the projector and the language model (fully or with
   adapters), sometimes the vision encoder too, on visual question answering, document,
   chart and grounding data in conversational form.

Larger systems train all parts jointly on interleaved image-text data from the start.

**Design consequences.**

- Abilities are capped by what the vision encoder preserves. A contrastively trained
  encoder keeps semantics and loses fine spatial detail, which limits counting, small
  text and localisation.
- Many images or video frames exhaust the context quickly; frame sampling and
  per-frame token compression are required.
- The language model's priors are strong, so the model can answer plausibly without
  using the image at all.

**Follow-ups**

- How many tokens does a 1344 by 1344 image cost with tiling, and what does that do to latency?
- Why freeze the language model in the first stage?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-029">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> To bring images or audio into a transformer, you can use continuous embeddings from an encoder or discrete tokens from a learned codebook. Compare the two.</summary>

**Continuous embeddings.** An encoder maps the input to a sequence of real-valued
vectors, which a projector feeds into the model.

- Preserve information well, with no quantisation loss.
- Natural for *understanding*: the model reads them and outputs text.
- Not directly usable as an *output*: the language model's head predicts a distribution
  over a finite vocabulary, and a continuous vector has no such distribution. Generating
  the modality needs something extra, such as a regression or diffusion head, or a
  separate generator conditioned on the model's output.

**Discrete tokens.** A tokenizer for the modality (a vector-quantised autoencoder for
images, a neural audio codec with residual quantisation for sound) maps the input to
indices in a learned codebook, and a decoder maps indices back to pixels or waveform.

- The modality becomes "just more tokens". One autoregressive model with one
  cross-entropy loss can read and write text, image and audio tokens, in any
  interleaving.
- Quantisation loses detail. Reconstruction quality is bounded by the tokenizer, and
  fine textures, small text or audio fidelity suffer unless many tokens are used.
- Sequences are long: hundreds to thousands of tokens per image, and tens to hundreds
  per second of audio, often several parallel codebook streams.
- Codebooks are hard to train: some entries may go unused.

**How systems combine them.**

- Understanding-only models: continuous embeddings in, text out.
- Generation: discrete tokens predicted autoregressively, or a diffusion or flow model
  operating in a continuous latent space, conditioned on text or on the language
  model's hidden states.
- Unified models often read with continuous features, which are better for perception,
  and write with discrete tokens or a diffusion head, which are better for generation.

**Deciding.** If the product only needs to interpret the modality, use continuous
embeddings from a strong pretrained encoder. If it must generate it with tight coupling
to language, such as speech-to-speech with low latency or interleaved image and text,
discrete tokens or a jointly trained continuous head are needed, and the tokenizer's
rate and quality become the central design choice.

**Follow-ups**

- Why can a language model head not output a continuous embedding directly?
- What sets the token rate of an audio codec, and why does it matter for a voice model?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-030">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Your vision-language model describes objects that are not in the image and answers some questions the same way whatever image is shown. How do you diagnose and reduce this?</summary>

The model is leaning on its language prior. The language model is far stronger than the
visual pathway, and for many questions a plausible answer exists without looking: "what
colour is the banana?", or a kitchen scene that "should" contain a fridge.

**Diagnose.**

- *Blind baseline.* Run the evaluation with the image removed or replaced by a blank or
  random image. The score that survives is what language alone achieves, and the gap to
  the real score is what vision contributes.
- *Counterfactual images.* Edit an image so the usual answer is wrong (a blue banana) or
  pair each question with two images that require different answers. Consistency on
  such pairs measures grounding.
- *Existence probes.* Ask about objects that are absent but typical for the scene, and
  measure the rate of false "yes" answers.
- *Attention to image tokens.* Where the model allows it, check how much the answer
  changes when image tokens are perturbed.
- *Slice by what is asked.* Counting, spatial relations, small text and fine detail fail
  for a different reason: the vision encoder or the resolution loses the information.

**Reduce.**

- *Resolution and encoder.* If the detail is not in the visual tokens, no training of
  the language model will recover it. Raise the resolution, tile, or use an encoder
  that preserves spatial detail.
- *Training data.* Add examples where the prior is wrong: counterfactual and negative
  examples, questions about absent objects with "no" as the answer, and unanswerable
  questions with abstention as the target. Balance the data so that the answer cannot
  be guessed from the question.
- *Training recipe.* Make sure the projector and language model were trained enough on
  grounded tasks, and that long, fluent captions do not dominate the data, since they
  reward plausible elaboration.
- *Inference.* Ask for the evidence, such as the region or the text that was read,
  before the answer; lower the temperature; shorten descriptions, since hallucination
  rises with length.
- *Evaluation.* Keep the blind baseline and the counterfactual pairs as permanent
  metrics.

For document and chart tasks, compare with a pipeline that extracts text first; if it
wins, resolution is the bottleneck.

**Follow-ups**

- The blind baseline scores 60% on your benchmark. What does that say about the benchmark?
- Why do longer captions contain more hallucinated objects?

</details>


### Post-training (RLHF, preference tuning, RL fine-tuning) <span class="demand">12% of postings</span> {#post-training}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.post-training.0"> Describe the RLHF pipeline and the role of the reward model and the KL penalty
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.post-training.1"> Derive the DPO loss from the KL-regularised objective and implement it
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.post-training.2"> Explain policy-gradient fine-tuning with a verifiable reward and a group baseline
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.post-training.3"> Name the failure modes of optimising a learned reward and how to detect them
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.post-training.4"> Describe how intended model behaviour is specified, trained and evaluated

<details class="qa" id="llm-014">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Walk through reinforcement learning from human feedback as originally practised. What are the stages, what is each loss, and what is the KL term for?</summary>

**Stage 1: supervised fine-tuning.** Train the pretrained model on demonstrations of the
desired behaviour (prompt and good response) with the usual next-token loss. This gives
a policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ that follows instructions.

**Stage 2: reward model.** Collect comparisons: for a prompt $x$, humans say which of two
responses is better. Train a model $r_\phi(x, y)$ that outputs a scalar, with the
pairwise (Bradley-Terry) loss

$$\mathcal L(\phi) = -\,\mathbb E\big[\log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)\big],$$

where $y_w$ is the preferred response. Comparisons are used because people are more
consistent at ranking than at absolute scoring.

**Stage 3: RL against the reward model.** Treat generating a response as an episode: the
policy samples a response, the reward model scores it, and the policy is updated with a
policy-gradient method (PPO in the original recipe) to maximise

$$\mathbb E_{x,\ y \sim \pi_\theta}\big[r_\phi(x, y)\big] \;-\; \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big).$$

**What the KL term is for.** The reward model is accurate only near the distribution of
responses it was trained on. Unconstrained, the policy finds outputs that score highly
for the wrong reasons, and drifts into degenerate text. The penalty keeps the policy
close to the reference model, where the reward model can be trusted and where language
quality is preserved. $\beta$ sets the trade between reward and drift.

**Why RL at all, instead of more supervised data?** Demonstrations show one good answer;
preferences can rank outputs the model itself produces, including on prompts where no
one wrote a reference, and the optimisation targets the judged quality directly.

**Weaknesses.** The reward model is a bottleneck and a target for exploitation; rater
disagreement and bias are learned; on-policy RL on long sequences is expensive and
unstable. These motivated simpler preference-optimisation methods that skip the
explicit reward model and the sampling loop.

**Follow-ups**

- What does the policy do if the KL coefficient is set to zero?
- Why are pairwise comparisons preferred over 1-to-5 ratings?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-015">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">derivation</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Derive the DPO loss. How does it turn preference data into a supervised objective without a reward model?</summary>

**Start from the RLHF objective** for a fixed reward $r$:

$$\max_\pi\ \mathbb E_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}\big[r(x, y)\big] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big).$$

**Its optimum has a closed form:**

$$\pi^*(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\, \exp\!\big(r(x, y) / \beta\big).$$

**Invert it** to express the reward through the optimal policy:

$$r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x).$$

**Substitute into the preference model.** Under Bradley-Terry, the probability that $y_w$
is preferred to $y_l$ is $\sigma\big(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)\big)$. The intractable
$\log Z(x)$ depends only on $x$ and cancels in the difference. Parameterising the policy
as $\pi_\theta$ and maximising the likelihood of the observed preferences gives

$$\mathcal L_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb E\left[\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \left[\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}\right]\right)\right].$$

**Reading it.** The policy is its own implicit reward model: the log-ratio to the
reference plays the role of the reward. The loss raises the likelihood of the preferred
response relative to the reference and lowers that of the rejected one, and the
reference model in the ratio is what is left of the KL constraint.

**What you gain.** No reward model, no sampling during training, no RL machinery: a
classification-style loss over fixed pairs, with two forward passes of the policy and
two of the frozen reference per example.

**What you lose or must watch.**

- It is offline. The model learns only from the pairs given; it never explores its own
  outputs, so the data must cover the behaviour you care about. Pairs generated by the
  current model are most useful.
- The loss can be reduced by lowering the rejected response's likelihood without
  raising the preferred one's, so monitor both log-probabilities.
- $\beta$ controls how far the policy may move; too small and it drifts into degenerate
  text.
- Noisy or inconsistent preferences are fitted as confidently as clean ones.

**Follow-ups**

- Why does the partition function cancel?
- Both log-probabilities are falling during training but the loss improves. Is that a problem?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-016">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Implement the DPO loss in PyTorch, including how you compute the log-probability of a response under a causal language model.</summary>

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def response_logp(model, input_ids, attention_mask, response_mask):
    """input_ids: [B, T] prompt followed by response.
    response_mask: [B, T], 1 on response tokens. Returns [B] summed log-prob."""
    logits = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask).logits
    logp = F.log_softmax(logits[:, :-1].float(), dim=-1)     # predicts token t+1
    tgt = input_ids[:, 1:]
    tok_logp = logp.gather(-1, tgt.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)
    return (tok_logp * response_mask[:, 1:]).sum(-1)

def dpo_loss(policy, ref, chosen, rejected, beta=0.1):
    """chosen / rejected: dicts with input_ids, attention_mask, response_mask."""
    pi_w = response_logp(policy, **chosen)
    pi_l = response_logp(policy, **rejected)
    with torch.no_grad():
        ref_w = response_logp(ref, **chosen)
        ref_l = response_logp(ref, **rejected)
    margin = (pi_w - ref_w) - (pi_l - ref_l)
    loss = -F.logsigmoid(beta * margin).mean()
    return loss, {"margin": margin.mean(), "pi_w": pi_w.mean(), "pi_l": pi_l.mean()}
```

What an interviewer checks:

- **The shift.** Logits at position $t$ predict token $t + 1$, so drop the last logit and
  the first label, and shift the mask the same way.
- **Mask to the response.** Only response tokens count; the prompt is conditioning. The
  mask also removes padding.
- **Sum, not mean, over tokens.** The derivation is about the log-probability of the
  whole response. Averaging per token changes the objective and its length behaviour.
- **The reference is frozen** and evaluated without gradients. Its log-probabilities can
  be precomputed once for a fixed dataset.
- **Numerics.** Use `logsigmoid`, and compute the log-softmax in full precision when the
  model runs in half precision.
- **Logging.** Track the chosen and rejected log-probabilities separately, and the share
  of pairs with positive margin. A falling loss with both log-probabilities falling
  means the model is degrading its outputs.

Memory: a naive step holds four forward passes. Concatenate chosen and rejected into one
batch per model, and cache the reference values.

**Follow-ups**

- What breaks if you average the log-probability over tokens instead of summing?
- How would you precompute the reference terms, and when does that become invalid?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-017">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> When would you fine-tune a language model with reinforcement learning on a task reward, instead of supervised fine-tuning or preference optimisation? How do policy-gradient methods with a group baseline work?</summary>

**Choose by the signal you have.**

- *Demonstrations* of good outputs: supervised fine-tuning. Simple and stable, but the
  model can at best imitate the demonstrations.
- *Comparisons* between outputs: preference optimisation such as DPO. Offline and
  cheap, limited to the pairs collected.
- *A reward you can compute on any output*: reinforcement learning. Examples are unit
  tests that pass or fail, a checkable final answer, a task completed in an
  environment, or a trusted grader. RL lets the model improve on its own samples, so it
  can exceed the demonstration data and learn multi-step strategies no one wrote down.

RL is worth its cost when such a reward exists, when it is hard to exploit, and when
supervised data has stopped improving the model.

**How it works for text.** A response (or a multi-step trajectory) is an episode; its
tokens are actions; the reward arrives at the end. The policy gradient weights each
sampled response's log-probability by its advantage.

**Group baseline.** Training a value network for long token sequences is difficult.
Instead, sample a group of $G$ responses for the same prompt, score them, and normalise
within the group:

$$A_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}{\operatorname{std}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}.$$

Responses better than their siblings are reinforced, worse ones suppressed. The prompt's
difficulty cancels, and no critic is needed. The update is then a clipped,
PPO-style objective on the token log-probability ratios, usually with a KL term toward
a reference model. GRPO is the best-known method of this shape.

**What goes wrong.**

- If all samples for a prompt get the same reward, the advantage is zero and nothing is
  learned. The task distribution must be at the edge of the model's ability.
- Reward exploitation: the model finds outputs that satisfy the checker without solving
  the task.
- Collapse of diversity and drift in language quality without the KL term or a mix of
  supervised data.
- Cost: many samples per prompt, each of which may need an environment to score it.

Monitor reward, the fraction of solved prompts, KL to the reference, output length and a
held-out evaluation that the reward cannot see.

**Follow-ups**

- Every sample in a group scores zero. What does the model learn, and what do you change?
- Why is a learned critic hard for long token sequences?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-018">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> During RL or preference tuning against a learned reward model or an LLM judge, the reward keeps rising but human raters say the outputs are getting worse. What is happening and what do you do?</summary>

This is over-optimisation of a proxy. The reward model is an approximation fitted on a
limited distribution of outputs. The policy is an optimiser that searches for whatever
raises the score, and it moves into regions where the approximation is wrong.

**Typical exploits.**

- *Length and style.* Longer, more detailed-looking, more confident or more flattering
  answers score higher, regardless of correctness.
- *Surface markers.* Formatting, hedging phrases, lists, apologies, or keywords the
  reward model associates with quality.
- *Agreeing with the user* over being right.
- *Repetition or degenerate text* that happens to score well far from the training
  distribution.
- *Gaming a judge model*'s known preferences, including text addressed to the judge.

**Confirm.**

- Plot human-rated quality on a fixed sample against training steps, next to the reward.
  The point where they separate is where to stop.
- Compare output statistics over training: length, vocabulary diversity, frequency of
  particular phrases.
- Score outputs with a second, independent judge that was not used in training.
- Track the KL divergence from the reference policy; a large value means the policy has
  left the region where the reward model was fitted.

**Fix.**

- Constrain the policy: a larger KL coefficient, fewer steps, early stopping at the
  divergence point.
- Improve the reward: collect human labels on the *current* policy's outputs and retrain
  the reward model, iterating. Use an ensemble and optimise a conservative statistic.
  Normalise or penalise length explicitly.
- Combine signals: verifiable checks where they exist, and a mix of supervised data to
  anchor language quality.
- Keep a held-out human evaluation and an independent automatic judge as release gates
  that the optimisation never touches.

The general principle: once a measure is optimised directly, it needs an independent
measure to check it.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you detect a length bias in a reward model before training against it?
- Why does retraining the reward model on the current policy's outputs help?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-019">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> How is the intended behaviour of an assistant model (what it helps with, what it refuses, its tone and honesty) specified and trained in? Describe the loop from specification to evaluation.</summary>

Behaviour is shaped in layers, and the hard part is keeping them consistent.

**1. A written specification.** A document stating what the model should do: priorities
when goals conflict (for example safety, then honesty, then helpfulness), what content
is declined and why, how to handle uncertainty, tone, and how instructions from the
system prompt, the user and tool outputs rank. Published examples include model specs
and constitutions. Its value is that people labelling data, writing evaluations and
reviewing failures work from the same text.

**2. Data that demonstrates it.** Supervised examples and preference comparisons
constructed or labelled according to the specification, covering clear cases and,
deliberately, borderline ones. Much of this data is now generated and graded by models
following the specification, with human review of samples and of disagreements.

**3. Training.** Supervised fine-tuning, preference optimisation and RL against graders
derived from the specification. Reasons and principles in the data generalise better
than bare rules, which the model applies too broadly or too narrowly.

**4. Run-time layers.** The system prompt adjusts behaviour within what training allows;
classifiers and filters around the model catch what training missed. Training gives
robust defaults; prompts give flexibility; filters give a backstop.

**5. Evaluation.** Suites for each behaviour, measured in both directions: harmful
compliance and over-refusal of benign requests, since pushing one down raises the
other. Add adversarial testing, consistency across paraphrases, and checks that general
capability did not regress.

**6. Iteration.** Failures found in evaluation or production are traced to a gap in the
specification, in the data or in training, and fixed at that layer.

**Trade-offs to name.** Rules against judgement; refusal rate against helpfulness;
robustness to adversarial prompts against steerability by legitimate operators; and
the limits of verification, because behaviour on a test suite does not prove behaviour
everywhere.

Be clear about which parts you have worked on directly and which you know from
published accounts.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you measure over-refusal?
- Why might training on explanations generalise better than training on rules?

</details>


### Model architecture and scaling research <span class="demand">12% of postings</span> {#model-arch-research}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.model-arch-research.0"> State what scaling laws say about loss as a function of parameters, data and compute
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.model-arch-research.1"> Design a fair small-scale comparison for an architecture change
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.model-arch-research.2"> Explain mixture-of-experts layers and their trade-offs

<details class="qa" id="llm-038">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What do scaling laws for language models say, and how do practitioners use them?</summary>

**The empirical finding.** For transformer language models, test loss falls smoothly and
predictably as a power law in each of three quantities, when the other two are not the
bottleneck: the number of parameters $N$, the number of training tokens $D$, and the
training compute $C$. Schematically, $L(N) \approx L_\infty + (N_0 / N)^{\alpha}$, with
similar forms for data and compute. The trends hold over many orders of magnitude and
are fairly insensitive to architectural details within the transformer family.

**Compute-optimal allocation.** For a fixed compute budget $C \approx 6ND$, how should it
be split between model size and data? An early analysis favoured growing the model much
faster than the data. A later one, with learning-rate schedules matched to each run
length, found that parameters and tokens should grow roughly in proportion, at about 20
tokens per parameter for the models studied, which implied that many large models of
the time had been under-trained.

**How they are used.**

- *Planning.* Fit the curve on small and medium runs and extrapolate the loss of a
  larger run before paying for it. A run that lands off the curve signals a bug or a
  bottleneck.
- *Comparing ideas.* An architectural or data change is worth adopting if it shifts the
  curve (better loss at equal compute across scales), not if it wins at one small size.
- *Budgeting.* Choosing $N$ and $D$ for a compute budget, and deciding whether more
  data or a larger model is the better purchase.

**Caveats.**

- The laws describe pretraining loss. The relation between loss and downstream ability
  is monotone but not linear; some abilities appear abruptly.
- Exponents and the optimal ratio depend on data quality, tokenizer and architecture.
  Treat published constants as specific to their setup.
- Training cost is not the only cost. A model served at high volume should be smaller
  and trained longer than the compute-optimal point, because inference cost scales with
  $N$. Many current small models are trained far beyond 20 tokens per parameter for
  this reason.
- Extrapolation far beyond the fitted range is a forecast, not a law.
- Data is finite: at some point high-quality tokens, not compute, are the constraint.

**Follow-ups**

- Why would you deliberately train a model that is smaller than compute-optimal?
- A new architecture beats the baseline at 50 million parameters. What else do you need to see?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-039">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> You have an idea for an architectural change to a transformer and a small compute budget. How do you test it so that the result means something at larger scale?</summary>

Most architecture ideas that win at small scale do not survive scaling or fair tuning.
The experimental design has to be built around that fact.

**1. A strong, tuned baseline.** Use a well-known baseline implementation and tune its
learning rate, warm-up and regularisation at each scale you test. A common cause of
false positives is a new method that was tuned against a baseline that was not.

**2. Equalise what matters.** Compare at equal parameters, equal training compute and
equal wall-clock on the same hardware, and report all three. A change that adds
parameters or FLOPs must beat a baseline enlarged by the same amount. Keep data,
tokenizer, context length and evaluation identical.

**3. Tune both arms equally.** Give each the same hyperparameter search budget. The
optimal learning rate often shifts with an architectural change; comparing at one
shared learning rate can favour either side arbitrarily.

**4. Several scales.** Run at least three model sizes spanning an order of magnitude or
more and look at the trend. A gain that is constant or growing with scale is promising.
A gain that shrinks is the usual fate: many tricks are compensations for small models
or short training.

**5. Noise.** Run several seeds at the small scales to learn the run-to-run variance,
and compare differences with it.

**6. Look beyond the final loss.** Training curves (does it only converge faster?),
stability across learning rates, throughput and memory, behaviour at longer context,
and downstream evaluations. A change that improves loss per step but slows each step
may lose at equal wall-clock.

**7. Ablate.** If the idea has several parts, remove each to find which carries the
effect. Often it is one small part, or an incidental change such as initialisation.

**8. Check the implementation.** Unit-test the new component, verify it reduces to the
baseline when switched off, and overfit a tiny dataset.

**9. Decide in advance** what result would count as success and what would end the
project, to resist reading noise as signal.

Report negative results and the conditions honestly. For a reader deciding whether to
spend a large run on the idea, the scaling trend and the fairness of the baseline are
the whole question.

**Follow-ups**

- Your method adds 5% parameters and improves loss by 1%. How do you make the comparison fair?
- Why can sharing one learning rate between baseline and variant mislead in either direction?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-040">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What is a mixture-of-experts transformer layer? What does it buy, and what does it make harder in training and serving?</summary>

**The layer.** In a standard transformer block every token passes through the same
feed-forward network. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer replaces it with $E$ feed-forward
"experts" and a small **router**. For each token the router scores the experts, the
top $k$ (often 1 to 8 of dozens or more) are evaluated, and their outputs are combined
with the router's weights. Attention layers stay shared.

**What it buys.** Parameters and compute are decoupled. The model has $E$ experts' worth
of feed-forward parameters, but each token pays for only $k$ of them. At a fixed
compute per token, the model has far more capacity than a dense one, and at equal
quality it needs fewer FLOPs per token.

**What it makes harder in training.**

- *Load balance.* Without pressure, the router sends most tokens to a few experts and
  the rest are never trained. An auxiliary balancing loss, noise in routing or capacity
  limits per expert are used.
- *Discrete routing.* The top-k choice is not differentiable; the router learns only
  through the experts it selected, which adds instability.
- *Uneven batches per expert.* Each expert sees a variable number of tokens per step,
  which complicates batching and, in distributed training, means tokens must be sent to
  the devices holding their experts. Communication and stragglers become design
  problems.
- *More hyperparameters*: number of experts, k, where to place MoE layers, the balancing
  coefficient.

**What it makes harder in serving.**

- *Memory.* All experts must be loaded even though each token uses few, so the memory
  footprint is that of the full parameter count. The savings are in compute, not in
  memory.
- *Batching efficiency.* Tokens in a batch go to different experts, so each expert
  processes a small, irregular sub-batch. Throughput gains are smaller than the FLOP
  count suggests unless the implementation groups tokens by expert well.
- *Quantization and fine-tuning* interact with routing: an adapter or a domain shift can
  change which experts are used.

**Interpretation.** Experts rarely correspond to human-recognisable topics; routing
tends to follow token-level and syntactic patterns.

**When to consider it.** Large models where training and inference compute, not memory,
is the constraint. For small models and memory-limited deployment, a dense model is
usually simpler and as good.

**Follow-ups**

- Why does an MoE model not save memory at inference?
- What happens if the load-balancing loss is too strong?

</details>


### Distillation and model compression <span class="demand">6% of postings</span> {#distillation}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.distillation.0"> Write the distillation loss with temperature and explain the factor of temperature squared
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.distillation.1"> Choose between logit-level and sequence-level distillation for a language model

<details class="qa" id="llm-020">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Write the knowledge distillation loss with temperature in PyTorch and explain each part. Why is the soft term multiplied by the temperature squared?</summary>

A small student is trained to match a large teacher's output distribution as well as the
labels:

$$\mathcal L = \alpha\, \mathrm{CE}\big(y, \sigma(z_s)\big) + (1 - \alpha)\, T^2\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\sigma(z_t / T)\,\|\,\sigma(z_s / T)\big),$$

with student logits $z_s$, teacher logits $z_t$, softmax $\sigma$ and temperature $T$.

```python
import torch.nn.functional as F

def distillation_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, labels, T=2.0, alpha=0.5):
    hard = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)
    soft = F.kl_div(
        F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1),     # log q
        F.softmax(teacher_logits.detach() / T, dim=-1),  # p
        reduction="batchmean") * (T * T)
    return alpha * hard + (1 - alpha) * soft
```

**Why soft targets help.** The teacher's distribution says more than the label: which
wrong classes are nearly right and by how much. That is many more bits of supervision
per example, and it acts as a regulariser.

**Temperature.** Dividing logits by $T > 1$ flattens the distribution, so the small
probabilities of non-target classes, where this extra information lives, contribute to
the loss. Typical values are 1 to 5.

**The factor $T^2$.** The gradient of the soft term with respect to the student's logits
scales as $1/T^2$: one factor of $1/T$ from the scaled logits, and another because the
softened distributions differ less. Multiplying by $T^2$ keeps the soft term's gradient
magnitude comparable to the hard term's when $T$ changes, so that $\alpha$ keeps its
meaning.

**Pitfalls.**

- `F.kl_div` expects log-probabilities as its first argument and probabilities as its
  second; swapping them or passing raw logits fails silently.
- `reduction="batchmean"` gives the true KL per example; the default averages over
  classes as well.
- Detach the teacher and run it in evaluation mode.
- For sequence models, apply the loss per token and mask padding.

Beyond logits, students can also match intermediate features or attention maps, which
needs a projection when dimensions differ.

**Follow-ups**

- Show where the factor of one over temperature squared comes from.
- When does a student trained with distillation outperform one trained on labels alone, and why?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-021">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> You want a small, cheap model that performs like a large one on your task. Compare distilling from logits with training on the large model's generated outputs. What decides the quality of the result?</summary>

**Logit-level distillation.** The student is trained to match the teacher's
next-token distribution at every position, on some corpus.

- Needs access to the teacher's full output distributions, so the teacher must be a
  model you run. Vocabularies must match or be mapped.
- Rich signal per token; efficient in data.
- Storing teacher distributions for a large vocabulary is expensive; in practice the
  teacher runs alongside the student or only the top-k probabilities are kept.

**Sequence-level distillation.** The teacher generates responses to a set of prompts,
and the student is fine-tuned on them with the ordinary next-token loss.

- Works with any teacher, including one behind an API, subject to its terms of use,
  which may forbid this.
- The student sees only one sample from the teacher's distribution per prompt, so it is
  less informative per example, but it is simple and scales with generation budget.
- The teacher can be prompted elaborately, with reasoning, retrieval, several attempts
  and self-checks, and only the final answer kept. The student learns to produce in one
  cheap pass what took the teacher an expensive pipeline. This is the main reason the
  approach is so widely used.

**What decides quality.**

- *The prompts.* The student is good where the distillation inputs cover. Use real task
  inputs, not only synthetic ones, and match production's distribution of difficulty.
- *Filtering.* Teacher outputs contain errors; keep only those that pass verification
  (tests, a judge, agreement across samples). A student trained on unfiltered outputs
  inherits and amplifies mistakes.
- *Student capacity.* A narrow task distils into a small model well. A broad capability
  does not compress without loss, and the gap shows up on hard and rare inputs.
- *Starting point.* Begin from a pretrained small model, not from scratch.
- *Evaluation.* Compare student and teacher on held-out real inputs, by slice, and
  measure the cost and latency actually achieved.

A typical production result: a model ten or more times cheaper that matches the teacher
on the bulk of traffic, with a router sending the hard remainder to the large model.

**Follow-ups**

- Why can a student trained on filtered teacher outputs end up better than the raw teacher on the task?
- How do you decide which requests still go to the large model?

</details>


### Interpretability and explainability <span class="demand">6% of postings</span> {#interp}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.interp.0"> Distinguish attribution, probing and mechanistic methods by the question each answers
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.interp.1"> Explain superposition and what a sparse autoencoder is trained to do
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.interp.2"> Use Shapley-value explanations for a tabular model and state their limits

<details class="qa" id="llm-033">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Give an overview of interpretability methods for neural networks. What question does each family answer, and how far can each be trusted?</summary>

Four families, each answering a different question.

**1. Attribution: which inputs mattered for this output?** Gradient-based saliency,
integrated gradients, attention visualisation, occlusion, and Shapley-value methods.
They produce a score per input feature or token. Cheap and widely used, but different
methods often disagree, some are insensitive to the model's weights, and attention
weights are not explanations. Check them with perturbation: removing the highly
attributed inputs should change the output.

**2. Probing: is this information present in the representations?** Train a simple
classifier on a layer's activations to predict a property (part of speech, the truth of
a statement, the position of an object). High accuracy shows the information is
decodable. It does not show that the model uses it, and a powerful probe can learn the
task itself, so control tasks and simple probes are needed.

**3. Causal interventions: does this component cause the behaviour?** Ablate or patch
activations: run the model on one input, replace an internal activation with the one
from a different input, and see whether the output changes accordingly. Steering adds a
direction to activations to change behaviour. These tests give evidence of mechanism,
because they manipulate the computation rather than observe it.

**4. Mechanistic interpretability: what algorithm do the weights implement?** Decompose
activations into interpretable features, with sparse autoencoders and related methods,
and trace circuits of features and attention heads that compute a behaviour. The most
ambitious family, and the least complete: results cover selected behaviours, and the
decompositions leave part of the computation unexplained.

**Behavioural explanation** stands beside these: asking the model to explain itself.
It is easy and useful to users, and it is not a reliable account of the internal
computation.

**How to use them.**

- Debugging a model or dataset: attribution and example-based methods to find spurious
  features, verified by intervention.
- Auditing for a property: probing plus causal tests.
- Research on model internals and safety: features and circuits.

The trust rule: an interpretation is a hypothesis about the model, and it should make a
prediction that an intervention can confirm or refute.

**Follow-ups**

- Why is a high-accuracy probe not evidence that the model uses the feature?
- How would you check that a saliency map is faithful to the model?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-034">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What is superposition, and what is a sparse autoencoder trained to do in interpretability research? What are the method's limits?</summary>

**The problem.** Individual neurons in a network usually respond to several unrelated
things, so reading neurons one at a time does not reveal clean concepts.

**Superposition** is the leading explanation. A model benefits from representing many
more features than it has dimensions. If features are sparse, meaning few are active at
once, the model can assign them directions that are almost, but not exactly,
orthogonal, and tolerate the small interference. Features are then directions in
activation space that do not line up with neurons.

**Sparse autoencoders (SAEs).** To recover those directions, train an autoencoder on a
layer's activations $x \in \mathbb R^d$ with a hidden layer much wider than $d$ and a
sparsity pressure:

$$f = \operatorname{ReLU}\big(W_e (x - b_d) + b_e\big), \qquad \hat x = W_d f + b_d,$$

$$\mathcal L = \lVert x - \hat x \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert f \rVert_1.$$

Each activation is reconstructed as a sparse combination of a large dictionary of
directions, the columns of $W_d$. The hope is that each dictionary element is one
feature the model uses. Variants replace the L1 penalty with a top-k or gated
activation to control sparsity directly.

**How it is evaluated.**

- Reconstruction: error, and how much the model's loss worsens when $\hat x$ replaces
  $x$ in the forward pass.
- Sparsity: average number of active features per input.
- Interpretability: whether the inputs that activate a feature share a meaning people
  or models can describe, and whether intervening on the feature changes the model's
  behaviour as that meaning predicts.

**What it is used for.** Finding features for specific concepts, steering or ablating
them, and tracing circuits in terms of features instead of neurons.

**Limits.**

- Reconstruction is imperfect, and the unexplained residual may contain what matters.
- The features depend on the dictionary size and the training run: larger dictionaries
  split a feature into finer ones, so there is no single canonical set.
- An interpretable feature is not proven to be the unit the model computes with; causal
  tests are still required.
- Training dictionaries for every layer of a large model is expensive.
- It is an active research area, and claims about what has been understood should be
  stated with their scope.

**Follow-ups**

- Why does sparsity of features make superposition possible?
- How would you test that a feature labelled with a concept really represents that concept?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llm-035">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> A regulator or a customer asks why your model made a particular decision. What can Shapley-value explanations tell them, where do they mislead, and what are the alternatives?</summary>

**What SHAP gives.** For one prediction, each feature receives an attribution $\phi_i$,
its average marginal contribution to the output over all orders in which features could
be added, such that

$$f(x) = \mathbb E[f(X)] + \sum_i \phi_i.$$

The attributions add up exactly to the difference between this prediction and the
average prediction. For tree ensembles they can be computed exactly and quickly; for
other models they are approximated by sampling. Averaging absolute values over a dataset
gives a global importance ranking.

**Where they mislead.**

- *They explain the model, not the world.* A large attribution means the model relies on
  the feature, not that the feature causes the outcome. Presenting it as causal advice
  ("raise your income and you will be approved") is wrong unless the model is causal.
- *Correlated features.* Computing a marginal contribution requires evaluating the model
  with some features "absent", which is done by substituting values from a background
  distribution. With correlated features this evaluates combinations that never occur,
  and credit is split among correlated features in ways that depend on the method.
- *The baseline matters.* Attributions are relative to the background data chosen.
- *Stability.* Sampling-based estimates vary between runs, and similar inputs can get
  different explanations.
- *Proxies.* A protected attribute can act through correlated features without
  appearing itself.

**Alternatives and complements.**

- *An interpretable model.* Linear models, scorecards, shallow trees, or boosted models
  with monotonic constraints. Where decisions must be explained and contested, a
  slightly less accurate model that can be read directly is often the right choice.
- *Counterfactual explanations.* The smallest change to the input that flips the
  decision, restricted to features the person can change. This is what people
  want to know.
- *Global views.* Partial dependence and accumulated local effects for how a feature
  moves the prediction; permutation importance for reliance.
- *Example-based.* Similar past cases and their outcomes.

**In a regulated setting.** Find out what the rule requires, such as specific reasons for
an adverse decision; validate explanations for stability and for consistency with
monotonic expectations; document the method and its limits; and test for disparate
impact separately, since an explanation does not establish fairness.

**Follow-ups**

- Two features are almost perfectly correlated. How will their attributions behave?
- Why might you choose a monotonic boosted model over a more accurate unconstrained one?

</details>


### Synthetic data and data generation pipelines <span class="demand">5% of postings</span> {#synthetic-data}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.synthetic-data.0"> Design a generate, filter and verify pipeline and say what makes its output trustworthy
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.synthetic-data.1"> Explain the risks of training on model outputs and how to measure diversity and quality
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llm.synthetic-data.2"> Design a data flywheel from production traffic with a labelling and evaluation loop

<details class="qa" id="llm-022">
